extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society / natural philosophers, experimentalists, and astronomers of the late 17th century
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and reasoning from experimental and observational natural-philosophy work (field observations, laboratory/shipboard experiments, dissections, and astronomical calculations) with procedural steps and evidential criteria. Includes how to perform, observe, and interpret experiments and transits, and how to use ancient sources and physical data to reconstruct historical events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of lunar phase, tides, and wind to date and locate historical landings
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine dates and landing places by correlating reported lunar phases (full moon dates), tidal times (high/low water), and prevailing wind directions mentioned in sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example application: infer that a reported full-moon at night must be Aug 30 and that a landing '4 days before the full-moon' in the afternoon with flood tide setting northward implies landing in the Downs north of the cliffs. Combine tidal timing (high-water ~8am, low-water ~2pm) with reported sailing time (3pm) to deduce whether the commander sailed with or against the tide. Use wind descriptions (e.g. 'leni Africo' = S.W.) and historical sailing capabilities (ships sail ~8 points off the wind) to test whether proposed embarkation ports and courses are consistent. Anti-pattern: relying on single ambiguous phrase without cross-checking tide/wind/latitude/time data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of ancient coastal places using classical geographers and measured distances
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate candidate identifications (e.g., Portus Icius, Gessoriacum) by comparing Ptolemy's place-names/latitudes, distances between named locations, and classical statements of stadia/miles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Ptolemy's stated latitudes/longitudes and reported distances (stadia) to test whether an ancient port aligns with modern sites; cross-check with other authors (Pliny, Dion Cassius, the Itinerary of Antoninus). Where classical distances conflict with modern surveys, prefer multiple converging data points (e.g., measured modern distance 26 English miles supports Caesar's estimate). Be cautious about later authors (250+ years after events) and correct for terminological differences (e.g., words meaning 'water's edge' vs 'marsh').

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipe/procedure for curing 'castorium' (preparation protocol)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical stepwise method to cure beaver 'stones' (castor-related material): extract milk, boil in water with wood ashes, smoke over birch-bark, and dry until hard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps: get milk out of the stones as cleanly as possible; boil them in water with half a shovel full of clean wood ashes for half a quarter of an hour; tie stones in pairs and smoke over birch-bark for ~1 hour until well dried in smoke; hang for a week or more until perfectly dry and hard; then pack for sale. If batch too large, repeat boiling with proportionate fresh ashes. Note: author flags terminology issue ('The term beaver.stones (teites) is exceedingly improper'). This is a production protocol—follow steps and drying times; anti-pattern: insufficient smoking/drying leading to spoilage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collection, processing, and propagation methods for cochineal production
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical and observational guidance for identifying the insect producing cochineal and for harvesting/processing it and propagating its host plant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identification: insect is coccus cacti (Linnaeus' coccus cacti), often mistaken for lady-bird species. Collection: when mature, smother insects by creating smoke to windward of shrubs with cloths spread beneath; shake plants to dislodge insects onto cloths. Processing: spread insects on cloths on sandy ground or pavement and sun-dry until bodies shrivel; rub between hands to crumble into grains and remove wings (garble); alternatively dry in broad shallow copper basins to speed drying. Propagation: propagate Indian fig (prickly pear) by placing single leaf in ground to root or by seed/fruit grains; note possibilities/questions about using eggs/grains or maggot stage for tincture. Guidance includes correcting taxonomic error and recommending experimentation on timing of collection (seasons) and drying methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and replication of shipboard bottle/flask experiments to probe water pressure at depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental procedure and interpretative criteria for assessing the effect of depth pressure on containers: vary stoppers (tender cork, hard cork, leather, ox bladder covers), create holes, change depths, and observe whether bottles come up full, partially full, or broken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from trials: a bottle 70 fathoms down with a good tender cork had the cork come up inside the bottle and was ~3/4 full; a bottle with hard cork remained but cork bruised; a bottle covered by four-fold ox bladder came up empty; adding leather increased resistance; making a pea-sized hole led to water ingress at 75 fathoms; single bladder survived 30 fathoms but broke at 50; repeating with double bladder survived 50 but broke at 75. Further tests used Florence flasks, open vs stopped, tied mouth-down: open flask filled with water while stopped flask broke at shallower depths. Guidance: vary stopper material, number of bladder layers, include leather backing, create controlled perforations to probe leakage thresholds, replicate at multiple depths and sea locations, and interpret differences as due to pressure and mechanical abrasion in descent. Anti-pattern: single trial, no control (open flask) or failing to note orientation or stoppage differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphological and behavioral criteria to identify hydatides as living worms (lumbrici hydropici) rather than simple cysts or eggs
rubrics_metrics.description: Set of observational features from dissection and microscopy used to argue that hydatides found in morbid animal bodies are a species of worm: structure of outer chorion and inner bladder, neck with orifice and rings, movable neck response to stimulus, presence of internal strings, and typical attachment sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key observations: hydatide enclosed in an outward membrane (chorion) loosely so inner bladder drops out retaining liquid; inner bladder has a neck or white protuberant body with an evident orifice composed of circular rings (seen more clearly under microscope and granulated with fine eminences); neck can protrude and retract when stimulated (e.g., near candle); inside neck two small strings float in the liquor (possible nutritive vessels); hydatides usually hang from membranous parts (omentum, peritoneum) rather than embedded in viscera. Guidance: perform repeated dissections across specimens (rotting sheep, antelope, living hydropical patient) and use microscopy and comparative anatomy (compare to known worms like taenia, leech stomachs) before concluding. Consider alternative hypothesis (egg/embryo) and seek more perfect/varied specimens; anti-pattern: concluding from single specimen or failing to use magnification to reveal rings/neck movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles and computational method for predicting visible conjunctions (transits) of inferior planets
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria determining when Mercury and Venus are seen entering the sun's disk and the calculation method to predict times, distances from sun center, visibility, and durations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fundamental condition: transits occur in conjunctions when the planet is retrograde and the sun is so near the planet's node that the planet's latitude at conjunction does not exceed the semidiameter of the sun. Treat each planet separately because elements differ. Use accurate node longitudes, orbital inclinations, planet-sun and planet-earth distances, and short-interval motions (e.g., motion in 6 hours) to compute apparent motion and visible path angle. From computed distance from sun center derive semi-duration (half-duration) of transit; add/subtract tabled semi-duration values (given per minute of distance) to the moment of conjunction to get beginning and end. Use observed epochal transits (e.g., Oct 28, 1677) to refine calculations; produce tables of conjunction years, local times, and distances, and mark which transits are partially or entirely visible at a given location. Guidance: combine the 'subtilest calculations' with observational industry for epoch determination; anti-pattern: using mean elements without accounting for nodes, inclination differences, or lacking local longitude/time corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording and adjusting observed transit times for longitude and local observation conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting observed transits, record the exact midpoint times at the observer's location and adjust for longitude differences when comparing distant observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Halley observed the middle of Mercury's transit at St. Helena at 4 m. p.m. (local) but at London it corresponded to 28 m. p.m.; provide both local times and corrected comparisons. Also record the planet's displacement from sun center (e.g., 4'40" north) to compare with computed distances. Guidance: accurate epochal observations improve predictive tables; include whether the transit is partly or wholly visible at the reporting location (use symbols to indicate partial/entire visibility).
